doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Family, identity and the Two Flowers metaphor
title: Father's death in the 1956 plane crash and the cemetery refusal
summary: His father, a rising executive, died in 1956; the family was refused cemetery services, and his mother suffered a breakdown, the story coming later from his father's friends.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: was the period of the McCarthy period. And if you were a Chinese-American you were suspicious of being a Communist and so forth. I actually had an FBI investigation, but mainly because he worked for the chemical plants and so he received Q Clearance, which was the highest clearance. But anyway he died in this plane crash in 1956, a two airplane crash. And when my family tried to hold services at the Glendale Cemetery I think — was it in Burbank or Glendale — I was only two years old — they refused us services. Even though my father’s body wasn’t going to be buried there, because it was burned to ashes in the fire in the plane crash. So we ended up in the Hollywood Hills. So that described the experience to me even though I didn’t understand a thing when I was two years old, as kind of what my mother had to go through raising three of us. Because there was two of us before my dad died, and then 8-1/2 months later my sister was born. So it evoked this image of my mother as being a lily that can endure in the swamp of racism. So and I guess that’s part of the meaning of “Two Flowers on a Stem.”

It’s a nice metaphor. It must have been difficult for her to convey what that was like to you once you were old enough to understand it. Is that how you learned about the incident with the cemetery and all that, from her?
No. I mean she withdrew and even entered depression and suffered a nervous breakdown and it was told actually years later by friends of my father.
